title: Sensors, communication & IoT networking
summary: Build the complete sensor-to-action chain, then learn which radio, network and messaging protocol carries each part of it. This week supplies the language used throughout the course.

sections.title: From a physical change to a useful action
sections.intro: A connected factory is a chain of functions. Learn the role of each box before memorizing protocol names.
paragraphs: A sensor observes a physical quantity such as temperature, gas concentration, light, pressure or movement and converts it into a signal. A processor reads that signal, applies a rule or algorithm and produces a decision. An actuator uses energy and a control signal to change the physical world: turn a motor, open a valve, switch a relay or sound a warning.

A transducer converts energy from one form to another. Sensors and actuators are both transducers, but their directions differ: a microphone turns sound into an electrical signal; a speaker turns an electrical signal into sound. A sensor output can be an electrical change in voltage, current, resistance or capacitance; it often needs processing before a person can understand it.

IoT connects physical objects to networks so their data can support useful services. IIoT applies this idea to factories, mines, plants and other industrial settings, where reliability and safety matter. Sensing and actuation are the endpoints; communication links them to processing that may be local, at a gateway or in a cloud.
keyPoints: Sensor → processor → actuator is the essential chain.

DHT22 measures temperature/humidity; HC-SR04 measures distance; PIR detects motion.

sections.title: How to describe and classify a sensor
sections.intro: A sensor can measure the right quantity and still be unsuitable if its range, response or precision is wrong.
paragraphs: Static characteristics describe measurements after the sensor has settled. Range is the lower-to-upper interval it can measure. Accuracy describes closeness to a reference. Resolution is the smallest detectable input change. Error is the difference from the reference. Sensitivity is change in output divided by change in input; linearity describes how closely the calibration curve follows a straight line.

Drift is a slowly changing reading under unchanged conditions. Repeatability is how consistently the sensor reproduces a reading under the same conditions. Dynamic characteristics describe what happens while an input changes: a zero-order model follows immediately; a first-order model approaches its final value gradually; a second-order model can overshoot or oscillate before settling.

Analog and digital describe the output interface. An analog signal varies continuously; a digital sensor provides discrete values or a binary state, often after internal conversion. Scalar and vector describe the quantity: temperature or gas concentration has magnitude; acceleration and magnetic field have magnitude and direction. A sensor can therefore be digital and vector at the same time.

The course uses an active/passive classification in which radar, sounder and altimeter actively interrogate an environment, while examples such as temperature and soil-moisture sensing are passive. This terminology has other conventions in instrumentation, so interpret it in the course context rather than assuming every textbook uses the same definition.

sections.title: IEEE 802.15.4 and ZigBee: the radio foundation
sections.intro: Separate the low-level radio rulebook from the higher-level network built on it.
paragraphs: IEEE 802.15.4 defines the physical and MAC layers for low-rate wireless personal area networks. The physical layer describes radio bands and modulation; the MAC layer controls access to the shared medium and frames. Low cost, low power and modest throughput make it suitable for small battery-operated sensors. The course associates it with DSSS coding and CSMA/CA medium access.

DSSS spreads a signal using a code sequence, which helps it resist some interference. CSMA/CA means a device checks the medium and tries to avoid transmitting over another device. In the original course band mapping, the lower 868/915 MHz bands use BPSK at 20–40 kbps, and the 2.4 GHz band uses O-QPSK at 250 kbps. Do not confuse a coding scheme, a modulation method and a MAC access method.

ZigBee builds networking and application functions above IEEE 802.15.4. A coordinator starts the network; routers relay messages over several hops; end devices do not route other devices’ packets. End devices can send as well as receive their own application data. Star, tree and mesh arrangements are possible, and ZigBee PRO improves network scalability, routing and security capabilities.

The notes list 802.15.4 variants as a recognition aid: b for higher-rate improvements, a for extended-range alternatives, c for China, d for Japan, e for industrial MAC improvements, f for active-RFID use and g for smart utility networks. Treat these as lecture associations, not as a complete modern standards catalog.

sections.title: 6LoWPAN, heterogeneous networks and service discovery
sections.intro: A common IP language helps unlike devices connect, but tiny radio frames need an adaptation layer.
paragraphs: IoT devices often have little memory, processing power and battery energy. Their networks can have small payloads, packet losses and changing routes. Heterogeneity means devices, vendors, access technologies, traffic and protocols differ. A proprietary non-IP gateway may tie a user to a vendor-specific API, reduce interoperability and limit scalable last-mile connection.

6LoWPAN means IPv6 over Low-power Wireless Personal Area Networks. IPv6 requires support for a 1280-byte minimum MTU, while the course’s IEEE 802.15.4 frame limit is 127 bytes. The adaptation layer between MAC and the IP network layer compresses headers and fragments packets into smaller pieces; the receiving side reassembles them. The original IPv6 header is 40 bytes and a UDP header is 8 bytes.

In mesh-under, forwarding is handled below IP in the adaptation layer using link-layer addresses. In route-over, each routing hop is at the IP network layer using IP addresses. The source emphasizes stateless address autoconfiguration and link-layer AES-128 security, and gives 2400–2483.5 MHz as the worldwide radio band for the assignment.

Three IETF efforts divide the job: 6LoWPAN adapts IP to low-power links; ROLL addresses routing in low-power and lossy networks; CoRE addresses web-style services on constrained devices. For service discovery, a device registers its resources through a Registration Interface, a Resource Directory stores descriptions, and a client uses a lookup interface to find them. REST-based protocols such as CoAP support these interactions.

Its key tasks: header compression, fragmentation and reassembly.

sections.title: Industrial wireless and home-control radios
sections.intro: A factory radio often values predictable delivery more than maximum speed.
paragraphs: WirelessHART is an industrial protocol based on IEEE 802.15.4. HART expands to Highway Addressable Remote Transducer. The course gives 2.4 GHz ISM operation, 250 kbps, DSSS, O-QPSK and channels 11–26. Time Division Multiple Access assigns transmission slots, while channel hopping reduces repeated exposure to an interfered channel. The source describes 100 slots per second; this is a useful timing figure rather than a universal fixed superframe length.

ISA 100.11a was developed by the International Society of Automation for industrial monitoring and process control. It uses an 802.15.4 foundation, supports IPv6 and AES-128, and emphasizes interoperability across different industrial protocols. The course lists star/mesh and TDMA/CSMA-CA operation.

Z-Wave is associated with home automation, locks, alarms and appliance control. Its sub-GHz bands avoid the busy 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi/Bluetooth environment. The course answer for maximum data rate is 100 kbps, with about 30 m range and 232 nodes in the described system. A four-byte Home ID identifies a network and a one-byte Node ID identifies a device. Mesh routing can bypass radio dead spots.

sections.title: Bluetooth, RFID and NFC
sections.intro: These technologies solve different jobs: replace a cable, identify an item, or exchange data with a tap.
paragraphs: Bluetooth connects nearby devices and peripherals. In the classic Bluetooth model used by the notes, a piconet has one master and up to seven active slaves; linked piconets form a scatternet. The source gives a 2.4 GHz band, 1–3 Mbps, and class ranges of approximately 1, 10 and 100 m. These are version/class-dependent lecture figures, not specifications for every Bluetooth device.

RFID has a tag, reader and supporting software. The tag contains an integrated circuit and antenna. A passive tag gets energy from the reader; an active tag has its own battery. Radio identification does not require an optical line of sight like a barcode scanner, which is useful for tracking parts, baggage, livestock and shipments.

NFC is a very-short-range technology related to RFID. The course gives under 10 cm, 13.56 MHz and rates of 106, 212 or 424 kbps. Its close interaction is useful for contactless payment, access and device pairing. The notes describe active-active and active-passive modes: an active device supplies an RF field, while a passive interaction relies on the other device’s field.

sections.title: Networks and Quality of Service
sections.intro: Delivering a value is useful only if it arrives in time, stays valid and fits the receiver’s limits.
paragraphs: A typical implementation connects sensor motes to a local network and gateway, then to internet/cloud services for storage and analytics, and finally back to an actuator. A mote commonly includes a sensor, processor and radio. A gateway bridges the local technology to the wider network. Applications are the leaves, the architecture is the trunk and device/protocol choices are the roots of the notes’ IoT tree analogy.

Quality of Service describes delivery and resource properties. Resource utilization controls memory and bandwidth: resource limits restrict buffering and time filters restrict sampling or arrival rate. Timeliness controls freshness: a deadline limits gaps between updates, while a latency budget limits time from send to receive.

Data availability controls what usable information is retained: durability keeps data available after its publisher disappears; lifespan sets how long a sample remains valid; history sets how many old samples are kept. Data delivery covers reliability and transport priority. These four groups can be remembered as Resource, Timeliness, Availability, Delivery.

Network requirements can compete: broad coverage, high throughput, low latency, high reliability and power efficiency. Sending continuously may improve freshness but drain batteries; buffering may preserve samples but use memory. Choose policies for the application rather than assuming every reading needs the strongest possible guarantee.

sections.title: Application protocols: MQTT, CoAP and DDS
sections.intro: Radio carries bits; an application protocol defines how devices and applications exchange meaningful messages.
paragraphs: MQTT uses publish/subscribe over TCP. A publisher sends a message to a broker under a topic name; subscribers ask the broker for topics they want. Publisher and subscriber do not need to know one another directly. QoS 0 is at most once: no protocol acknowledgment or retry. QoS 1 is at least once: retries can produce duplicates. QoS 2 provides exactly-once delivery for the protocol exchange using a stronger handshake; it does not by itself guarantee exactly one business action across an entire system.

CoAP is a constrained REST-style protocol associated with IETF CoRE. The assignment answer for its transport is UDP. A client accesses resources through request/response operations; confirmable messages can be acknowledged, non-confirmable messages avoid that exchange, and acknowledgment/reset are message types. DTLS is a security protocol used for datagram transport. The notes’ methods list is simplified: Observe is an extension and PUSH is not a standard core CoAP method.

DDS RTPS is a data-centric real-time publish/subscribe protocol over UDP. The data is organized around topics; subscribers express interest in topics and QoS policies can address deadlines, reliability, persistence and freshness. AMQP supports messaging with delivery guarantees and flow control; the source associates it with financial systems. XMPP is XML-based messaging with extensibility and federated servers; it is not inherently a serverless network. IEEE 1888 is presented as URI-based exchange for environment monitoring and energy management.

The final assignment’s OSI session-layer question has DTLS as its supplied key. This is a course-key mapping, not a precise universal OSI placement: DTLS secures datagram communications and is commonly discussed with transport security. Keep the answer for this assignment and the technical meaning separate. The source also associates XMPP with DTLS; conventional XMPP transport security is typically TLS.

title: Industry 4.0, Lean & the smart factory
summary: Understand why industry connects machines, how Lean removes waste and how data creates business value. Connect these ideas to the flexible, self-adapting smart factory.

sections.title: Four revolutions, four different enabling ideas
sections.intro: The exam often checks whether a technology belongs to the correct industrial era.
paragraphs: The first industrial revolution mechanized production using steam power and railways, broadly from the 1760s to the 1840s in these notes. The second used electricity and mass production in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. The third introduced computers, semiconductors and information technology into manufacturing from the 1960s onward. The fourth connects sensors, machines, computation and people so production can respond intelligently.

Industry 4.0 is associated with Germany, and the course dates the term to the Hannover Fair in 2011. Smart means a machine can detect conditions and adapt its behavior; connected means it exchanges information over networks. Both matter: a clever isolated controller cannot coordinate an entire supply chain.

The course calls the fourth revolution the Second Machine Age, associated with Erik Brynjolfsson and Andrew McAfee. Lower-cost sensors, smaller computers, stronger networks and AI make it possible. Digital goods can have very low replication and distribution cost, while physical goods still have material and logistics costs. Historical examples include smartphone growth and platform businesses; those illustrate disruption rather than current market statistics.

The steam engine is not a fourth-revolution characteristic.

sections.title: Megatrends and sustainable production
sections.intro: Industry 4.0 is driven by physical, digital and biological change, but lasting production must also conserve resources.
paragraphs: The physical megatrend includes autonomous vehicles, 3D printing, advanced robotics and new materials. The notes characterize new materials as lighter, stronger, recyclable and adaptive, with examples such as graphene and carbon nanotubes. These are desirable properties across new-material development, not a promise that every new material has every property.

The digital megatrend includes IoT, tracking through RFID/NFC, connected supply chains and blockchain-based transactions. The biological megatrend includes gene sequencing, DNA-related engineering and drug selection informed by molecular characteristics. The boundaries can overlap: manufacturing a customized medical implant combines digital design, physical fabrication and biological needs.

A sustainable industry seeks energy efficiency, resource conservation and low-waste production. It manages the whole process rather than only adding a digital device. Government subsidies can support projects, but reliance on a subsidy is not one of the lecture’s defining characteristics of sustainability. Renewable sources such as solar and wind can reduce dependence on fossil resources, while efficiency reduces the energy demanded in the first place.

sections.intro: ICT connects production, but technology decisions also face supply, energy, regulation and workforce pressures.
paragraphs: The source groups globalization issues into five areas: business models, energy prices, ICT adoption, supply-chain management and emerging markets. ERP supports shared planning and business information; wireless networks support mobility; GPS locates shipments; RFID identifies parts. Regulation may address labor, honest advertising, privacy, safety and environmental protection. Energy is produced, transferred, transformed and consumed, so efficiency opportunities exist across that chain, not only at the final machine.

The course uses simplified descriptions of economic downturns and historical population projections. The practical manufacturing response is to improve productivity and reduce cost while conserving resources. sections.title: Lean: create value and remove waste
sections.intro: Lean starts with what the customer values, then removes work that does not help deliver it.
paragraphs: Lean grew from Toyota’s production system in Japan. Its goals are high quality, lower cost and shorter production time with minimum waste. The two pillars are Jidoka and Just-in-Time. Jidoka stops or exposes a problem so defective output is not repeatedly produced. JIT makes what the next process needs, in the needed amount and at the needed time.

The seven wastes are Transportation, Inventory, Motion, Waiting, Overproduction, Over-processing and Defects: TIM WOOD. Transportation moves material/information unnecessarily; motion is unnecessary movement by people. Overproduction makes too much or too soon; over-processing adds work the customer does not value. A connected plant can use timestamps and sensor data to reveal these wastes, but collecting data alone does not remove them.

A value stream includes every action needed from the customer’s order through delivery. Some work creates customer value, some incidental work is currently necessary but does not add value, and some work is pure waste. Walking one value stream with stakeholders lets a team list and prioritize improvements, then schedule follow-up to see whether they worked.

Lean implementation has four dimensions: business requirements define objectives and strategy; performance management uses people management and KPIs; operational improvement uses appropriate tools; people engagement follows Learn, Do, Teach. Supporting approaches include quality management, flexible manufacturing, IT, virtual integration, Lean supply chains and JIT. Continuous improvement depends on people practicing and teaching, not just buying software.

sections.title: Smart products: monitor, control, optimize, automate
sections.intro: These four capabilities build on one another; the assignment asks what resource enables optimization.

Optimization applies algorithms to choose better operating conditions: improve performance, scheduling, energy use or service. Automation combines monitoring, control and optimization so a product performs activities autonomously within its designed limits. Optimization algorithms are the resource linked to Optimization in the assignment.

Connected products can support faster production, lower costs, more effective recalls, improved supply-chain coordination and reduced environmental impact. Sensors and actuators supply measurements/actions, embedded systems provide local logic and communications, and cloud systems provide larger-scale processing and storage. Real-time monitoring improves visibility; the business must then use the information to create value.

sections.title: Business value and the three-layer architecture
sections.intro: The technology must connect a customer benefit to a workable way to earn revenue.
paragraphs: The course’s three key attributes of a smart business model are value proposition, revenue streams and technologies. The value proposition describes the benefit offered to a customer; revenue streams describe how money arrives; technologies explain what makes delivery possible. Four supporting building blocks are customer value, profit blueprint, key resources and key processes.

The four value-creation perspectives are novelty, efficiency, lock-in and complementarity. Novelty creates new services or markets. Efficiency reduces friction, delay and error. Lock-in encourages an ongoing customer relationship and makes migration harder. Complementarity combines products, services, technologies and online/offline activities so they create more value together.

The architecture has physical, connectivity and digital layers. Physical includes sensors, microcontrollers and microprocessors acquiring data. Connectivity carries it through technologies such as Wi-Fi, cellular, ZigBee or Bluetooth. Digital provides storage, algorithms and applications. These are different roles even when one device implements all three.

The source uses Amazon Dash Button as a historical lock-in example with a low-cost Wi-Fi device and mobile app, and Semios as an efficiency example with agricultural sensing, cellular communication and subscription monitoring. They illustrate the model and layer mapping. Workforce understanding matters: people need to know why a change is being introduced and how to use it.

paragraphs: The course defines a smart factory as a flexible system that can self-optimize across a broader network, adapt and learn from new conditions in real or near-real time, and run production processes autonomously. Smart machines, manufacturing processes, engineering, devices, IT and analytics work together to deliver smart products.

Five characteristics are Connection, Optimization, Transparency, Proactivity and Agility. Connection links machines, humans and data centers. Optimization improves scheduling, energy, throughput and reliability. Transparency gives a live understandable view of items and machines. Proactivity predicts issues before they stop production. Agility combines Flexibility, Adaptation and Self-configuration.

Big data handles high-volume, high-velocity, varied readings; cloud provides scalable storage and computation; a smart grid helps manage energy demand and load balancing. The automation pyramid moves from field/device level through control and manufacturing systems to ERP. AR and VR can support remote monitoring, training and safe work around dangerous equipment.

Expected gains include lower costs, better quality, improved predictability and worker safety. A physical ledger alone is not one of the course’s smart-factory components. It is the connected measurement, software and analysis that enable timely coordinated decisions.

sections.title: Cyber Physical Systems: the physical and cyber worlds interact
sections.intro: A CPS keeps reacting to a changing world; it is not a one-time calculation on stored data.
paragraphs: Cyber Physical Systems are interacting networks of physical and computational components, co-engineered as one system. Physical space contains machines, vehicles, people and processes. Cyber space contains computation and software, which may run locally, on a server or in a cloud. A CPS measures a physical state, computes a decision, applies control and then measures the result again.

An embedded system is computation built into a device, such as a washing-machine controller. Its core capabilities are compute, communicate and control. The course contrasts one embedded device with a broader CPS network of embedded and physical systems. A CPS still can have resource-constrained components; networking does not make every processor unlimited.

Reactive computation means ongoing interaction with the environment through input/output streams. Concurrency means several processes operate during overlapping time and may communicate synchronously or asynchronously. Real-time computation means a result must meet a timing requirement, not that computation takes zero time. Feedback and coordinated/hybrid control link software decisions to physical consequences.

CPS applications include image-guided surgery and therapy, robotic surgery, prosthetics and exoskeletons; traffic-signal coordination and collision warnings; smart meters and power-grid monitoring; and intelligent manufacturing machines. Safety, security, robustness, sensing, modeling, verification and training are challenges. Mobile CPS additionally face changing network stability, battery/power limits and security; design aesthetics is not a primary engineering constraint in the assignment.

sections.title: Smart and intelligent sensors
sections.intro: A local processor can do more than forward a raw measurement.
paragraphs: A smart sensor combines a sensing element with processing and communication. A typical path is sensing element, signal conditioning, analog-to-digital conversion and digital interface. Conditioning filters or amplifies the raw signal; the ADC changes it into numeric values. Multi-sensing, communication, computation and calibration functions can be integrated.

The notes draw a distinction between predefined smart-sensor functions and an intelligent sensor that can customize embedded algorithms, process sensed data and manage external sensors or devices. An intelligent sensor contains a microcontroller, memory such as flash/RAM/ROM and an application platform. Local processing can reduce the amount of data sent and support continuous monitoring.

Hardware constraints include power, response time, synchronization, bandwidth and security; software must be partitioned appropriately across applications and processors. Applications range from fault forecasting and automatic assembly to advanced driver assistance, intelligent textiles and chemical analysis. A more capable processor is useful only if the device can still meet its power and timing limits.

The smart-versus-intelligent distinction is the course’s conceptual comparison rather than a strict universal product taxonomy. The source first lists smart-sensor self-calibration and later says smart sensors need an external calibration processor. Drivers include shorter lifecycles, complex products, outsourcing and dispersed teams. The assignment asks for a 10-step PLM solution approach. sections.title: AR and VR: add to reality or enter a simulation
sections.intro: Both can support industrial work, but they change the user’s environment in different ways.
paragraphs: Augmented Reality enhances the present perception of the real world by adding computer-generated information. A maintenance technician can still see the machine while an overlay identifies a part or shows a measurement. Course device components include sensors, cameras, processing, projection/display and optical reflection arrangements; a remote control is the assignment’s non-component.

Four AR types are marker-based, marker-less, projection-based and superimposition-based. Marker-based AR recognizes a visual pattern. Marker-less AR can use location, compass or motion sensing. Projection-based AR places light on real surfaces. Superimposition uses object recognition to replace part of an observed view with additional content.

Virtual Reality creates an interactive artificial 3D environment, usually with visual, auditory and sometimes haptic feedback. Components include sensors such as accelerometers/gyroscopes, processing, lenses, displays and headsets. Non-immersive VR uses a screen/window, semi-immersive systems offer a partial immersive environment, and fully immersive systems use head-mounted displays and tracking.

Industry uses both for training, collaboration, assembly, safety, maintenance, factory planning and digital prototyping. AR can guide work on existing equipment; VR can let an operator practice a hazardous scenario before encountering it. The notes associate AR with Thomas Caudell and VR with Jaron Lanier; recognize these names without assuming one historical milestone describes every earlier system.

sections.title: AI, knowledge and learning
sections.intro: AI is a broad set of methods; this assignment emphasizes the older knowledge-base and heuristic-search model.
paragraphs: Artificial Intelligence studies computer systems that exhibit forms of intelligence, such as recognizing patterns, interpreting language, planning and decision making. The assignment attributes the phrase Artificial Intelligence to John McCarthy in 1956. The course examples include game playing, speech, computer vision, robotics, fraud detection and expert advice.

An algorithmic search follows a defined procedure; a heuristic uses rules of thumb to guide a search toward promising choices. The supplied contrast says a program with AI uses a large knowledge base and heuristic search, while a non-AI program uses a database and algorithmic search. This is an instructional contrast, not a universal test of whether modern software is AI.

Knowledge can be procedural (how to do something), declarative (facts/descriptions) or heuristic (rules of thumb). Machine Learning is a subset of AI that learns patterns from data; Deep Learning is a subset of ML using multilayer models that can learn representations. DL is not automatically the best method: data, compute, task and constraints influence the choice.

In IIoT, AI may help detect faults, reduce energy use, estimate demand or predict yield. The course lists challenges of connecting devices, understanding data, training models, making data accessible and making outputs actionable. Its NOT question chooses lack of available data because the lecture emphasizes abundant sensor output. In real applications, usable labeled or representative data can still be scarce; raw data volume alone does not solve training.

sections.title: Big data and its pipeline
sections.intro: A stream of industrial readings becomes valuable only after it is organized, cleaned and interpreted.
paragraphs: Big data refers to datasets and streams whose scale, speed or complexity exceed what ordinary tools can conveniently handle. Structured data has a defined schema, often tables; unstructured data such as images or free text does not naturally fit one fixed tabular schema. Industrial systems produce both, including time-series measurements, logs, images and maintenance notes.

The three main Vs are Volume, Velocity and Variety. The notes add Variability, Veracity, Visualization and Value. Volume is amount; velocity is arrival rate; variety is different formats; variability is changing meaning or behavior; veracity concerns trust, bias and noise; visualization presents data for understanding; value is the useful outcome extracted.

The pipeline collects data from sensors, logs and RFID; transmits it over networks; pre-processes it through integration, cleaning and redundancy reduction; stores it; and analyzes it. Inter-DCN transmission occurs between data centers, while intra-DCN transmission occurs within a data center. Removing repeated or irrelevant readings can reduce storage and bandwidth, but filters must preserve important events.

GFS and HDFS are distributed file systems for large-scale storage; the notes describe HDFS as open source and influenced by GFS. NoSQL denotes nonrelational database approaches and does not mean that data has no structure at all. Hadoop is a distributed storage/processing ecosystem, not one ordinary relational table. Traditional tools can still be useful for subsets, but large streams often require distributed approaches.

sections.title: Analytics, cloud and the final decision
sections.intro: Describe the past, predict the future, then recommend an action.
paragraphs: Descriptive analytics asks what happened, when and where. Predictive analytics uses patterns to estimate what may happen next. Prescriptive analytics considers what action is best under an objective and constraints. A temperature chart describes yesterday; a forecast estimates tomorrow; a scheduling recommendation prescribes how to respond.

Cloud computing supplies shared processing, storage and services on demand. The source’s five characteristics are on-demand self-service, broad network access, resource pooling, rapid elasticity and measured service. Elasticity means capacity can expand or contract with demand; measured service supports usage-based charging. This is scalable capacity, not literally infinite storage.

Industrial analytics should connect back to a CPS action or an informed human decision. A recommender system may suggest a product or maintenance step; an operator still needs useful context and appropriate safeguards. Hadoop and cloud can support large-scale computation, but the meaning and quality of data remain application responsibilities.

sections.title: Secure every part of the industrial chain
sections.intro: A connected machine is a physical process and an information system at the same time.
paragraphs: Cybersecurity protects hardware, software and data from unauthorized access, change or deletion. Physical security protects the real machines and facilities. A factory needs both: a corrupted command can damage equipment, and physical access to a device can compromise its software. Security, privacy and trust are related: protection, control over data exposure and confidence that information/system behavior is genuine.

The course lists five defense areas. Application security protects software applications; information/data security protects the data; network security protects communications and access; operational security protects the way information assets and business activities are handled; end-user education helps people recognize and avoid attacks. Application firewalls and suitable proxy/router controls can be countermeasures, but no single product provides complete security.

The CIA triad is Confidentiality, Integrity and Availability. Confidentiality prevents unauthorized disclosure. Integrity prevents unauthorized alteration. Availability means authorized users can obtain needed information/services when required. IIoT adds reliability and safety because a disrupted system can affect physical production and people. Authenticity, access control and non-repudiation also matter.

Legacy equipment may have been built before today’s security expectations. Connecting it can expose weak points, so protecting each device independently is not enough. Standards and coordinated design help address the whole chain. The notes mention a cyber-attack detection platform and Software Defined Cloud Manufacturing Architecture: software-plane tap points pass observations to an Ensemble Intelligence Framework to detect anomalies across software and hardware planes.

Social engineering manipulates people into violating a security policy or revealing protected information. The source names pretexting, where an attacker invents a plausible story or role, and watering-hole attacks, where a site expected to be visited by a target group is compromised. The common feature is exploitation of trust or behavior.

Phishing uses deceptive messages or sites that impersonate recognizable sources to steal credentials or other sensitive information. Spear phishing is targeted at a particular person or organization. Broad email phishing may be sent widely; spear phishing can use carefully selected details. The assignment’s statement reversing these two descriptions is False.

Users should understand how to identify suspicious requests and follow the organization’s verification procedure. Familiar branding alone is not proof that a message or login page is legitimate. The lecture examples of Google Docs and Dropbox phishing refer to imitation or abuse aimed at users, not a claim that those brands are inherently malicious.

sections.title: IIoT: connected automation and its adoption challenges
sections.intro: The change is not that factories suddenly gained sensors; it is that measurements and decisions can be coordinated across them.
paragraphs: IIoT applies IoT to industrial settings such as manufacturing, mining, agriculture and healthcare. Its goals include worker safety, ergonomics, longer machine life and operational efficiency. The professor describes it as traditional automation plus sensing, actuation and decision making in a connected manner.

The contrast with old automation has three parts. Sensing becomes ubiquitous rather than confined to one machine. Analytics combine data from many machines, sites and processes rather than a standalone local view. IT methods add shared communications, standardization opportunities and access to established hardware, software and skilled people. Connected data still needs useful analysis to produce a benefit.

Five adoption challenges are data integration, cybersecurity/privacy, lack of standardization, legacy installations and lack of skills. Device interoperability lets devices communicate; semantic interoperability means their data has mutually understood meaning, including units and context. A network can successfully carry two messages while the applications misunderstand them.

The coal-mine example measures hazardous gas and warns a control center/workers; roof/strata monitoring can give early collapse warnings, and RFID/location information can help locate miners. A hospital example sends body temperature and pulse-oximeter readings to a doctor’s screen. A pulse oximeter estimates oxygen saturation and pulse rate. Connected monitoring supports alerts, but the device is part of a larger safety or clinical procedure.

sections.title: Industrial sensors and the complete signal path
sections.intro: Factories need accurate, reliable measurements for long periods in harsh conditions and at a scale they can afford.
paragraphs: Industrial sensing must balance high performance, durability, low cost and reliable connectivity. The source shows methane, oxygen and carbon-monoxide sensors. It gives a methane operating range of about −20 to +55 °C with an example sensitivity around 24 ± 4 mV per percent methane; an electrochemical oxygen output about 0.1 ± 0.02 mA in air; and a CO range of about 20–2000 ppm. These are example-device figures, not specifications for every gas sensor.

The lecture’s smart-sensor configuration contains a multi-parameter sensing unit, analog detection circuit, digital signal conditioning unit and bus interface. Manual Control Unit is the assignment’s non-component. The sensor’s physical signal is detected and conditioned, the ADC turns analog into digital values, and a processor runs logic with memory and communication. A DAC can turn a digital command into an analog output for suitable actuation.

Calibration compares a sensor with a standard reference so bias or other errors can be adjusted or recorded. Conditioning, conversion and calibration are different: filtering prepares the signal; ADC changes representation; calibration establishes correspondence to a known reference. Industry-grade designs may perform sophisticated onboard corrections.

The milk-packaging example uses an impeller in the flow path. Flow spins the wheel; its electrical pulses/signals let the controller infer how much liquid has passed and stop filling at a threshold. Other applications use GPS for logistics, moisture/weather/nutrient sensors for agriculture, ECG/EMG/EEG and smart beds/pills in healthcare, and RFID in retail. The notes name Zephyr/Linux variants/Android Things, languages such as C/C++/Python, MRAA low-level interfaces and UPM higher-level sensor APIs as software examples.

sections.title: PLC, SCADA and industrial actuation
sections.intro: Local controllers execute the process; supervisory systems give operators a wider view.
paragraphs: A Programmable Logic Controller is a rugged special-purpose digital computer used to automate industrial equipment and processes. Its modules are CPU with memory, power supply and input/output. The I/O module connects analog/digital sensors and actuators. A PLC can participate in a connected IIoT system while retaining local control responsibilities.

The lecture’s scan cycle starts with monitoring/time housekeeping, reads inputs and their status, executes the user application, runs diagnostics, writes outputs and repeats. This repeated scan makes the relationship between current input and commanded output understandable. Timing and safe behavior still depend on the actual controller and process.

SCADA means Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition. It collects data from multiple sites, supports monitoring and analysis, and provides a supervisory view in water, oil and power systems. Course components are the supervisory system, Human Machine Interface, Remote Terminal Unit, communication interface, programming and PLC. SCADA and PLC are complementary roles, not competing names for exactly the same box.

Wireless sensor/actuator networks can ease installation and self-organization, but must still satisfy timing, reliability and security needs. Electro-hydrostatic actuation combines electric and hydraulic capabilities, with high force and decentralized control. Electro-pneumatic actuation combines electric control with compressed-fluid action for precise flow control, communications and diagnostics.

sections.title: Design a connected process and its 5C Control stage
sections.intro: Industry 3.0 automated isolated tasks; Industry 4.0 coordinates them and keeps people informed.
paragraphs: The course process timeline moves from mechanization to mass production, then computers/automation, then connected autonomous systems. The distinguishing 4.0 role is communication across machines and the supply chain. A lecture growth chart predicts the highest growth for electronics; the assignment answer is Electronics. The numerical growth percentages are predictions in the historical source, not present-day evidence.

An IIoT setup has four components: smart objects, networking infrastructure, business intelligence and people in the loop. Four design facets are interoperability, distributed decision making, information clarity and technical assistance. A machine may decide locally, while shared objectives and information coordinate the wider production system. Technical assistance uses smart objects to reduce unnecessary human burden, while people remain responsible for suitable decisions.

The final 5C stage is called Control in this lecture. It performs supervised control, self-configuration, self-optimization and self-adjustment. Earlier weeks call the related stage Configuration. Connection collects data, Conversion extracts information, Cyber links/aggregates the system, and Cognitive interpretation supports decisions before Control applies them.

Enablers are cloud platforms with IaaS/PaaS/SaaS, visualization, analysis and virtualization. Expected process features are efficiency, competitiveness, a skilled workforce, innovation and flexibility. Market volatility, workforce training, supply-chain flexibility, resource use and shorter product lifecycles remain practical challenges even after the devices are connected.
